```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

In vibe coding, a programmer describes what is wanted in natural language
and an AI assistant writes, runs and revises the code. The assistant's side
of such a session is a sequence of behaviours: it investigates the code base,
plans, executes changes, explains, reports results, asks questions, delegates
work and repairs what went wrong. How these behaviours are ordered says how
the assistant works. An assistant that investigates before it plans and plans
before it executes follows a different process from one that executes
repeatedly and repairs afterwards. The order of repairs is of particular
interest: a repair that follows execution suggests that the assistant
corrects its own failed actions, a repair that follows a report or an
explanation suggests that it corrects course after communicating with the
programmer.

Lag sequential analysis tests, for every ordered pair of behaviours, whether
the second follows the first more or less often than the frequencies of the
two behaviours predict (Bakeman & Quera, 2011). This case study asks what
follows what among the eight behaviour codes, what the coarser cluster level
adds, whether repair follows execution or reporting more than chance, and
how certain and stable the key transitions are.

```{r package}
library(lagdynamics)
```

## Data

`ai_long` is a long event log of coded AI behaviours in human-AI vibe-coding
sessions, taken from the Nestimate package. Each row is one coded behaviour
of the assistant.

- **Session:** `session_id` — one working session, the sequence boundary;
  sessions belong to a `project`.
- **Order:** `order_in_session` — the position of the event in its session.
- **Behaviour:** `code` — one of eight codes: `Ask`, `Delegate`, `Execute`,
  `Explain`, `Investigate`, `Plan`, `Repair`, `Report`.
- **Cluster:** `cluster` — the code's broader group: `Action`,
  `Communication` or `Repair`.
- **Message:** `message_id`, with `code_order` ordering several codes within
  one message.

```{r data}
head(ai_long)
with(ai_long, table(code, cluster))
```

The 8,551 events are dominated by `Execute` (3,258) and `Investigate`
(2,317), followed by `Plan` (1,620). `Ask` (99), `Report` (181) and `Repair`
(257) are rare. The cluster labels need care: the cluster called `Repair`
contains the `Repair` code and also `Plan`, and `Plan` makes up 1,620 of its
1,877 events. A transition into the `Repair` cluster is therefore mostly a
transition into planning.

```{r structure}
with(ai_long, c(projects = length(unique(project)),
                sessions = length(unique(session_id)),
                messages = length(unique(message_id))))
aggregate(cbind(events = order_in_session) ~ session_id, data = ai_long,
          FUN = length) |>
  summary()
with(ai_long, table(codes_per_message = table(message_id)))
```

The events come from 428 sessions in 34 projects. Sessions range from 1 to
138 coded events, with a median of 13. Of the 5,970 messages, 3,781 carry one
code and the others two to six. Within a message the codes are ordered by
`code_order` and follow each other in `order_in_session`, so some
transitions are between two codes of the same message rather than between
two messages. The analysis treats the coded order as the order of behaviour.

## What follows what?

`lsa()` reads the log in long format: `session` names the sequence
boundary, `action` the coded behaviour and `order` the position, so no
transition is counted across sessions.

```{r fit}
fit <- lsa(ai_long, session = "session_id", action = "code",
           order = "order_in_session")
fit
```

The fit has 8,123 transitions from 428 sessions. Independence is clearly
rejected (G² = 2,168, df = 49), and 40 of the 64 transitions depart
significantly from it. Sessions open with `Investigate` (71.5%) or
`Delegate` (18.5%). The over-represented transitions are the assistant's
working routines.

```{r over}
transitions(fit, direction = "over", sort = "strength") |> head(10)
```

The strongest routine is `Investigate` to `Plan`: 977 transitions against
442 expected (z = 33.4); 43.7% of investigations are followed by a plan.
`Delegate` to `Plan` follows (z = 18.1; 62.1% of delegations lead to a plan).
`Execute` repeats itself (z = 16.1; 51.0% of executions are followed by
another). Communication forms its own chain: a question is followed by an
explanation (`Ask` to `Explain`, z = 16.4, lift 7.51) and an explanation by
a report (`Explain` to `Report`, z = 14.0). `Plan` to `Execute` is
over-represented as well (z = 6.29), completing the routine of investigating,
planning and executing.

```{r under}
transitions(fit, direction = "under", sort = "strength") |> head(8)
```

The avoided transitions sharpen the routine. A plan is almost never followed
by another plan (49 against 298 expected, z = -17.9): planning is a single
step, not a loop. The assistant rarely executes straight after investigating
(z = -16.6) and rarely returns to planning after executing (z = -14.5): it
investigates, plans once, and then executes. `Repair` to `Plan` is almost
absent (4 against 49.6 expected).

A lag transition network shows the sixteen strongest residuals.

```{r network, fig.height = 5}
plot_transitions(fit, top = 16)
```

Each node is a behaviour and each arrow a transition, labelled with its
adjusted residual. Blue arrows are over-represented and red arrows avoided;
width grows with the size of the residual. Two clusters are visible. The
action routine runs from `Investigate` and `Delegate` into `Plan`, with the
thick blue arrow from `Investigate`, and from `Plan` to `Execute`, which
loops on itself. The communication chain runs from `Ask` to `Explain` and on
to `Report`. The red arrows mark the shortcuts the assistant avoids: from
`Investigate` directly to `Execute`, from `Execute` back to `Plan` and from
`Plan` to itself.

## The cluster-level view

The three clusters give a coarser description. The same call with
`action = "cluster"` fits the cluster sequence.

```{r cluster}
fit_cluster <- lsa(ai_long, session = "session_id", action = "cluster",
                   order = "order_in_session")
transitions(fit_cluster, sort = "strength")
```

All 9 cluster transitions are significant. `Action` to `Repair` is the
strongest (z = 20.6, 1,646 transitions), followed by `Communication`
repeating itself (z = 16.8) and `Repair` to `Action` (z = 14.0), while
`Repair` repeating itself is avoided (z = -18.5). Read with the cluster
labels alone, this would describe an assistant that acts, repairs and acts
again. The code-level fit shows what the clusters hide: `Action` to `Repair`
is mostly `Investigate`, `Delegate` and `Execute` followed by `Plan`, and the
avoided `Repair` loop reflects mainly the avoided `Plan` loop (49 plans
followed by a plan, against 298 expected). The cluster level is a
useful summary of the alternation between doing and planning, but a
statement about repair needs the codes.

## Does repair follow execution or reporting?

The question is answered on the `Repair` code. `lsa_lags()` fits the model
at lags 1 to 3, and `lag_profile()` follows the two candidate transitions.

```{r lags}
lags <- lsa_lags(ai_long, lags = 1:3, session = "session_id",
                 action = "code", order = "order_in_session")
lag_profile(lags, from = "Execute", to = "Repair")
lag_profile(lags, from = "Report", to = "Repair")
```

Repair does not follow execution more than chance. 93 executions, 3.0%, are
followed by a repair, close to the 97.8 expected (z = -0.62 at lag 1), and the residual stays between -1.6 and 0.5
at lags 2 and 3. A report, by contrast, is followed by a repair in 8.6% of
cases at lag 1 (14 transitions, z = 4.02, p < 0.001). The effect is
confined to the next event: at lags 2 and 3 the share falls to 2.6% and
4.2% and is not significant.

The full set of transitions into `Repair` shows which other behaviours
precede it.

```{r into-repair}
transitions(fit) |> subset(to == "Repair")
```

`Explain` to `Repair` is the strongest (42 transitions, z = 6.85, lift
2.63), followed by `Report` to `Repair` (lift 2.73). `Investigate` to
`Repair` is avoided (z = -4.36). Repair therefore follows the assistant's
communication, an explanation or a report, and not its actions. A repair is
in turn followed by an explanation (`Repair` to `Explain`, z = 7.01) or a
question (`Repair` to `Ask`, z = 5.90), as the over-represented transitions
above show. In these sessions repairs are embedded in the communication
with the programmer, consistent with a correction prompted by what the
programmer sees in the assistant's explanation or report.

## How certain are the key transitions?

`bootstrap_lsa()` resamples whole sessions with replacement, R = 1,000
times, and returns percentile intervals for every transition.

```{r bootstrap}
set.seed(2026)
boot <- bootstrap_lsa(fit, R = 1000)
boot
transitions(boot, significant = TRUE, sort = "strength") |> head(6)
```

42 of the 64 transitions have a residual interval that excludes zero. The
routines are certain: the residual of `Investigate` to `Plan` lies between
30.6 and 36.1, and the probability of a plan after an investigation between
0.408 and 0.467. The interval of `Ask` to `Explain` is the widest of the six
(11.6 to 21.1) because questions are rare, but it is far from zero.

```{r bootstrap-repair}
transitions(boot) |> subset(to == "Repair")
```

`Explain` to `Repair` has a residual interval of 3.90 to 10.00 and `Report`
to `Repair` one of 1.21 to 6.99; both exclude zero. `Execute` to `Repair`
has an interval of -2.51 to 1.47, which contains zero and is centred close
to it: there is no link between execution and repair to detect, rather than
a link too uncertain to establish. The interval of `Report` to `Repair` is
wide because it rests on 14 transitions, but its lower bound stays above 1.
`Plan` to `Repair` is the weakest over-represented transition into `Repair`;
its interval (0.05 to 4.03) barely excludes zero.

Stability asks the same question by subsampling. `stability_lsa()` refits
the model on R = 500 subsamples of 80% of the sessions.

```{r stability}
set.seed(2026)
stab <- stability_lsa(fit, R = 500)
stab
transitions(stab) |> subset(to == "Repair")
```

32 of the 64 transitions are significant in at least 95% of the subsamples.
`Explain` to `Repair` and `Investigate` to `Repair` are significant in all of
them and `Report` to `Repair` in 98.4%, so it passes the 95% threshold.
`Plan` to `Repair`, significant in the full fit at p = 0.046, is significant
in only 35.4% of subsamples and should not be interpreted.

## What the analysis shows

- The assistant follows a routine of investigating, planning once and
  executing: `Investigate` to `Plan` is the strongest transition
  (z = 33.4), planning does not repeat (z = -17.9), and execution repeats
  (z = 16.1).
- Communication is a separate chain: questions lead to explanations and
  explanations to reports.
- At the cluster level, the alternation between `Action` and the `Repair`
  cluster is mostly an alternation between action and planning, because the
  `Repair` cluster is mostly `Plan`.
- Repair does not follow execution more than chance (z = -0.62, bootstrap
  interval containing zero). It follows explanations and reports, at lag 1
  only, and is followed by further explanation or a question. The link from
  reports rests on 14 transitions but is stable in 98.4% of subsamples.

The analysis has limits. The data are coded behaviours of the assistant
only; the programmer's turns between them are not in the log, so a
transition from `Report` to `Repair` may pass through a programmer's reply
that the analysis cannot see. Several codes of one message are ordered by
the coding, not by time. The 428 sessions come from 34 projects, and the
bootstrap and the subsampling treat sessions as independent, which ignores
any similarity of sessions within a project. Finally, the model pools all
sessions: a project or a phase of a session with a different routine would
need a grouped fit (see [the group comparison article](group-comparison.html)).
For the long-format arguments, see [the event logs guide](event-logs.html);
for the network display, see
[the lag transition networks article](lag-transition-networks.html).

## References

Bakeman, R., & Quera, V. (2011). *Sequential analysis and observational
methods for the behavioral sciences*. Cambridge University Press.

Efron, B. (1979). Bootstrap methods: Another look at the jackknife.
*Annals of Statistics, 7*(1), 1-26.
